headline: High: Cline’s default workspace write/network/MCP powers create dangerous interaction paths with the unverified content-writing agent, especially for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no documented I/O surfaces, but B reads and writes workspace files, uses MCP, and runs browsers; if A’s content is placed into shared files or MCP-fed content, B can treat it as instructions. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty is escalated above low.
conditions: IF A’s output is copied into a workspace file that B reads
IF B ingests MCP or browser content without provenance filtering
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces
Disable MCP servers for B unless needed
Require a human review step before B acts on A-generated text
Tag A-originated files as untrusted in the workspace
requires-engineering: add provenance tracking between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: B touches source code, browser screenshots, and model-provider API keys, while A has broad network egress and is a content-writing agent with no documented isolation. If they share a workspace, B can read files that A influences, and A can exfiltrate content over the network. The shared-data pathway is plausible in default setups, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF A and B share the same filesystem workspace
IF B opens files that contain secrets or sensitive source code
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Store secrets outside shared project folders
Disable network egress for A when handling sensitive text
Review B’s workspace before launching browser tasks
requires-engineering: enforce OS-level sandboxing

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and shared-state-via-filesystem concurrency; A is unverified but has broad network egress and a content-writing role that can also mutate shared artifacts if given files. Because B’s defaults already permit concurrent writes in a shared workspace, conflict risk is high even though A’s write surface is not documented; uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF A is given write access to the same workspace as B
IF B modifies git state while A is producing or editing files
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate git branch
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use file locks for shared artifacts
Limit B to read-only mode during A’s runs
requires-engineering: add workspace-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: B can act on workspace content and browser-derived outputs, so if A produces unverified facts or instructions that B consumes, B may propagate errors into code or actions. A is a content-writing agent and B’s tool-using loop is approval-based but still operationally capable, making a default verification gap plausible rather than merely unusual.
conditions: IF B treats A’s text as authoritative input
IF B uses A-generated content to drive shell, browser, or MCP actions
mitigations: Require B to cite source files before acting
Insert a verification checklist before tool use
Mark A outputs as drafts only
Restrict B to read-only analysis until reviewed
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented for A, while B explicitly handles source code, browser screenshots, and model-provider API keys. The pair does not show a clear compliance breach by default, but B’s networked tooling and A’s broad egress create a small documented-gap risk if regulated data is introduced.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B’s workspace
IF A is used to generate or transmit jurisdiction-controlled content
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents
Review retention settings for B
Avoid sending secrets through A
Document data-class handling rules
requires-engineering: add residency controls
